o: Every liter gives 10 km. Every time 5 liters are consumed from the main tank, we gain 1 extra liter from the additional tank if available. So each 'block' of 5 liters effectively extends the journey. With mainTank, additionalTank ≤ 100, direct simulation is trivially fast. Example 1: consume 5 (50 km), refill to 1, consume 1 (10 km) → 60 km. Example 2: only 1 liter → 10 km. A closed-form also exists: each transfer converts 1 additional liter into 1 more main-tank liter, and transfers happen ⌊(mainTank−1)/5⌋ times at most, bounded by additionalTank.
k: Simulation is safe here because values are tiny (≤ 100).
Number of transfers = min(additionalTank, floor((mainTank-1)/5)); each transfer adds 10 km.

a.i: Repeatedly burn fuel: whenever the main tank has ≥ 5 liters, drive 50 km, spend 5, and pull 1 liter from the additional tank if possible; otherwise burn whatever remains at 10 km/L.
s: While mainTank ≥ 5: add 50 km, subtract 5 from mainTank, and if additionalTank > 0 move 1 liter over.
a.t: O(mainTank / 4) — each loop iteration consumes at least 4 net liters

a.i: Transfers occur after every 5 consumed liters except possibly the final partial tank, so the number of transfers is min(additionalTank, (mainTank-1)/5). Each transferred liter yields 10 km on top of mainTank×10 km.

w: Both work; prefer simulation in an interview for clarity, mention the formula as an optimization if constraints were huge. Pitfall: the formula uses (mainTank−1)//5, not mainTank//5, because the last group of 5 never triggers a useful refill once fuel runs out. Check mainTank=5, additionalTank=10 → 60 and mainTank=1 → 10.
